final_answer:
Short answer: On the stated facts, probably yes as to the dispersal order and the arrests, but the answer is fact-dependent and the facts as given leave the decisive issue open. The First Amendment does not bar police from dispersing an assembly; it bars dispersing or arresting people because they are engaged in peaceful, protected expression absent a sufficient justification. Whether the order was lawful turns on whether police had a genuine, articulable basis to find imminent unlawful conduct, not on a generalized worry.

1. Framework. Streets, sidewalks and plazas are traditional public forums where protest receives the strongest protection (Edwards v. South Carolina, 372 U.S. 229 (1963); Cox v. Louisiana, 379 U.S. 536 (1965); Ward v. Rock Against Racism, 491 U.S. 781 (1989); Frisby v. Schultz, 487 U.S. 474 (1988)). Content-neutral time, place and manner limits must be narrowly tailored to a significant governmental interest and leave open ample alternatives. Government may not punish speech merely because it is unpopular or might provoke a hostile reaction (Edwards; Cox; Terminiello v. Chicago, 337 U.S. 1 (1949)). Speech may be punished or dispersed only where it is directed to and likely to produce imminent lawless action (Brandenburg v. Ohio, 395 U.S. 444 (1969)). Edwards is closely analogous: about 200 people peacefully protesting on public grounds, ordered to disperse, arrests for breach of peace reversed because the state could not criminalize peaceful expression of unpopular views. Police concern about "potential for escalation" is the kind of generalized apprehension Edwards and Brandenburg reject; verbal arguments with passersby are protected or at most minor.

2. Traffic. Stepping into the street occasionally is a legitimate interest (traffic safety; Cox recognizes regulation of obstruction of streets) and can justify targeted enforcement (e.g., against individuals blocking traffic) or a narrowly tailored order to keep the roadway clear. It does not by itself justify declaring the entire assembly unlawful and ordering everyone off the plaza and sidewalk; that is overbroad relative to the interest. A permit requirement is a separate question (Chicago requires parade permits; not researched; Thomas v. Chicago Park District, 534 U.S. 316 (2002) allows content-neutral permit schemes, but spontaneous-event exceptions are a concern).

3. Illinois/Chicago law. Illinois mob action, 720 ILCS 5/25-1, requires use of force or violence disturbing the public peace, or assembly to commit a felony/misdemeanor or violence; a participant who does not withdraw when commanded by a peace officer commits a Class A misdemeanor (search summary; text not fetched). Chicago Municipal Code disorderly conduct provisions (and 720 ILCS 5/26-1) require conduct that actually disturbs or alarms the peace. A peaceful, mostly sidewalk-bound protest does not meet these elements, so an "unlawful assembly" declaration would be defective under the statute, which itself carries First Amendment significance (a failure-to-disperse arrest requires a lawful underlying order). Courts also require the law be applied narrowly (Grayned v. City of Rockford, 408 U.S. 104 (1972), upholding an anti-noise ordinance narrowly construed, and Coates v. Cincinnati, 402 U.S. 611 (1971), striking vague 'annoying' standard).

4. Arrests and probable cause. A failure-to-disperse arrest is lawful only if the dispersal order was itself lawful and probable cause existed. Courts distinguish: (a) where a crowd is acting as a unit and some members commit violence, police may disperse and arrest those who remain (Carr v. District of Columbia, 587 F.3d 401 (D.C. Cir. 2009) - persuasive, and it also stresses that dispersal orders and individualized probable cause matter; verified via search summary only); and (b) where there is no violence, mass arrest of peaceful protesters violates the First and Fourth Amendments (see, e.g., Collins v. Jordan, 110 F.3d 1363 (9th Cir. 1996) - persuasive, from memory, unverified). Seventh Circuit authority exists recognizing that public assembly rights yield to peace and order when genuine threats exist (a Seventh Circuit opinion surfaced in search but was not identified or verified). Remaining after a lawful order is not protected; but if the order was unconstitutional, a conviction/arrest on that basis is vulnerable, though Illinois does not generally recognize a right to resist even an unlawful order in all contexts, and qualified immunity (and Monell for the City) heavily shapes civil liability. Arguable probable cause for failure-to-disperse may shield individual officers even if the dispersal was unconstitutional (Reichle v. Howards, 566 U.S. 658 (2012); District of Columbia v. Wesby, 583 U.S. 48 (2018) - from memory).

5. Conclusion. If the facts are exactly as stated (peaceful, mostly on sidewalk, only verbal arguments, no violence, no imminent threat, only generalized concern), a court would likely hold the blanket unlawful-assembly declaration and arrests of those who remained violated the First Amendment (and likely the Fourth), at least for the City, given Edwards/Brandenburg. The City's best defenses: obstruction of the roadway, an unpermitted event, specific articulable threats not in the stem, or crowd acting as a unit with unlawful conduct (Carr); and individual officers likely will assert qualified immunity. Further facts needed: warnings given and audibility, dispersal routes, extent of street blocking, any permit, prior violence, and whether the 30 arrestees individually did anything unlawful. Note that I could not retrieve the full texts of most cited authorities due to network blocks; this is from background knowledge with limited verification, and subsequent history should be checked. I did not research post-2025 developments, including any Chicago litigation related to 2025 immigration protests.

issues.text: Whether a dispersal order of a mostly peaceful protest based on traffic and escalation concerns is a permissible content-neutral restriction or violates First Amendment
Whether arrests for failure to disperse are lawful (valid order, probable cause under Illinois mob action/disorderly conduct law)
Remedies/defenses: qualified immunity, Monell liability, crowd acting as unit

authorities.title: Edwards v. South Carolina
authorities.proposition: Peaceful protest of about 200 on public grounds could not be punished as breach of peace after dispersal order.

authorities.title: Brandenburg v. Ohio
authorities.proposition: Advocacy may be restricted only if directed to and likely to produce imminent lawless action.

authorities.title: Illinois mob action statute
authorities.proposition: Mob action requires force/violence or assembly for unlawful purpose; failure to withdraw on command is Class A misdemeanor.

authorities.citation: Carr v. District of Columbia, 587 F.3d 401 (D.C. Cir. 2009)
authorities.title: Carr v. District of Columbia
authorities.proposition: Police may arrest a crowd acting as a unit for some members' unlawful conduct; probable cause disputes preclude summary judgment.

authorities.title: Cox v. Louisiana
authorities.proposition: Streets may be regulated for traffic but peaceful demonstrators cannot be punished for fear of hostile reaction.

authorities.title: Collins v. Jordan
authorities.proposition: Dispersal of peaceful demonstrators based on others' potential violence violates First Amendment.

claims.text: Generalized concern about escalation does not justify dispersing a peaceful assembly absent imminent unlawful action.
Illinois mob action failure-to-withdraw requires an underlying mob action involving force/violence or unlawful purpose, absent on stated facts.
Where a crowd acts as a unit with unlawful conduct, police may disperse and arrest; persuasive authority.
Occasional street-stepping justifies targeted enforcement but not blanket dispersal.
